title: CFA Ethics 5: In-depth case studies - Standard I & II
subtitle: Professionalism and Integrity of Capital Markets, worked through real situations
whyItMatters: Standard I (Professionalism) and Standard II (Integrity of Capital Markets) are the two most heavily examined groups on CFA Level I, because their reach is so broad - this lesson works a separate case study for each sub-standard (I(A) through I(D), II(A) and II(B)) rather than lumping them together the way the overview lesson did.
openingQuestion: An analyst publicly attacks a rival firm on a personal social media account using unverified information, intending to damage the competitor's standing in the industry. Which sub-standard does this breach?
openingOptions: Standard I(D) Misconduct - it damages the profession's reputation
No violation at all, since this is a personal right to free expression
A violation only if the information is proved entirely untrue
Standard III, because it concerns duties owed to clients
explanation: Standard I(D) - Misconduct prohibits any conduct bearing on honesty or trustworthiness that could damage the reputation of the investment profession as a whole - including conduct on a personal social media account, away from the job itself. Publishing unverified information to damage a competitor's standing is a serious professional failing.

diagram.label: I(D) Misconduct → II(A) MNPI → II(B) Market Manipulation

realWorldExample.company: Share price manipulation through social media
realWorldExample.description: Cases around the world in which an influential individual posts false or wildly exaggerated claims about a stock on social media to drive the price up and then sell into it - the classic pump and dump - are textbook breaches of Standard II(B), Market Manipulation. It is among the violations that CFA Institute and regulators treat most severely, because it damages market integrity directly.

quiz.question: What does Standard I(A) - Knowledge of the Law require when local law and the CFA Institute Code of Ethics conflict?
options: Ignore both and decide for yourself on personal judgement
Follow only the Code of Ethics; local law does not matter
Always give local law priority and set the Code aside
Follow whichever of the two is the stricter standard
quiz.explanation: The rule in Standard I(A) is to follow the stricter of the two. If local law permits something the Code prohibits, a CFA member still has to follow the Code, because it is the stricter of the pair. If local law is stricter than the Code, the law governs. Neither one automatically outranks the other, which is why the two absolute answers are wrong in both directions. And personal judgement never replaces the comparison - the whole point of the rule is that it removes the discretion.

quiz.question: An analyst writes on a CV that they have 'completed CFA Levels I, II and III' when in fact they are still studying for Level II. Which Standard does this breach?
options: Standard I(C) Misrepresentation of professional qualifications
Standard VII, because it concerns the CFA examination programme
Standard II, because it touches the integrity of markets
No violation at all - that is just soft phrasing on a CV
quiz.explanation: Standard I(C) - Misrepresentation prohibits any misleading statement about education, work experience, professional credentials, or investment results. Overstating your CFA progress on a CV is a direct and serious breach. Standard VII does govern conduct as a candidate, but a false qualification claim is squarely a misrepresentation. Standard II concerns market integrity rather than personal credentials. And there is nothing soft about it: the claim is simply untrue, and CFA Institute is unforgiving about it.

quiz.question: A trader places a stream of fake buy and sell orders with no intention of having them filled, creating an illusion of heavy volume to draw other investors to a stock. What does this breach?
options: Standard V, since it relates to investment analysis generally
Standard II(B) Market Manipulation - manipulating the open market
No violation - this is simply a marketing technique for a stock
A violation only if those fake orders actually get executed
quiz.explanation: This is spoofing - placing orders you do not intend to fill in order to fake supply or demand - and it is a form of market manipulation prohibited directly by Standard II(B). The conduct distorts the market's natural price signal and misleads other investors who make decisions on the false picture. Execution is not required: the harm is done by the displayed order book, so waiting for a fill misunderstands the mechanism. And Standard V governs research and recommendations, which is not what is happening here.

quiz.question: Why does Standard I(B) - Independence and Objectivity stress refusing valuable gifts from a company you cover?
options: Because tax law bans accepting gifts of value in the finance industry
It only applies to cash gifts; gifts in kind raise no problem at all
Because a large gift creates a sense of obligation that bends your judgement
Because every gift is illegal in every single line of business there is
quiz.explanation: Behavioural research shows people reciprocate goodwill unconsciously, even when they sincerely believe themselves fully objective. Standard I(B) does not wait for evidence of actual influence before finding a breach - the mere EXISTENCE of a potential conflict is enough to require avoidance, protecting both real objectivity and how that objectivity looks from outside. The form the gift takes is irrelevant, since a lavish trip creates the same obligation as cash. And this is a professional standard, not a tax rule or a general prohibition on gifts.

quiz.question: What does Standard I(A) require when local law is looser than the CFA standard?
options: Apply the law of the country where the client is resident
Follow local law, since that is what has legal force here
Ask the certifying body before carrying out the transaction
Follow the stricter standard, which is the CFA standard
quiz.explanation: The rule is always to follow the stricter side. A looser law does not create permission to do what the standard prohibits - and where the law is stricter than the standard, the law naturally governs instead. The client's country of residence does not change the member's own obligation. And nothing requires you to seek a ruling from CFA Institute before acting, because the comparison itself is the test. This is the point in Standard I(A) that candidates most often get backwards.

keyTakeaways: Standard I(A) requires following the stricter of local law and the Code of Ethics, not automatically giving law priority
Standard I(C) - Misrepresentation covers false claims about your own qualifications and credentials, not just investment recommendations
Standard I(D) - Misconduct has a wide reach, including conduct outside work (such as social media) if it affects the profession's reputation
Standard II(B) - Market Manipulation includes manipulation through fake orders (spoofing), not only spreading false rumours

practicePrompt.question: Which of the following is correct according to this lesson?
options: Standard I(A) always requires local law to take priority, whether or not the Code is stricter
Standard I(D) Misconduct applies only during working hours and never to conduct outside work
Standard II(B) bans trading or statements meant to distort price or volume and mislead the market
A large gift from a covered company is always acceptable if the analyst believes it will not sway them
practicePrompt.explanation: Standard II(B) - Market Manipulation prohibits trading conduct or statements intended to distort price or trading volume in order to mislead the market. The other three each invert something the lesson establishes: Standard I(A) turns on whichever standard is stricter, Standard I(D) explicitly reaches conduct outside working hours, and Standard I(B) treats the existence of the conflict as sufficient regardless of how objective the analyst feels.

summary.keyIdea: Standards I and II cover a wide span, from personal conduct (a false CV, a public attack) to market conduct (spoofing, MNPI) - and the exam tests whether you can name the specific sub-standard
summary.commonMistake: Remembering only the group names 'Professionalism' and 'Integrity of Capital Markets' without being able to tell the sub-standards (A/B/C/D) inside each apart.
summary.action: In a case study, work out whether the conduct concerns law (I-A), objectivity (I-B), misrepresentation (I-C), misconduct generally (I-D), inside information (II-A) or market manipulation (II-B)

application.title: Practise classifying the sub-standards
application.message: Reread the four situations in the quiz and try drawing your own decision tree: Standard I or II? If I, is it A/B/C or D? If II, is it A or B?
application.secondary: Classifying sub-standards quickly and accurately is the core skill for the Ethics section of the CFA Level I exam.

sections.text: The earlier overview introduced Standards I and II in outline. This lesson goes deeper into each sub-standard - I(A) through I(D), II(A) and II(B) - through separate case studies, at the level of detail the CFA Level I exam actually tests.
Standard I(A): Knowledge of the Law - which one governs?

Where local law and the CFA Institute Code and Standards differ, the rule is to follow the STRICTER standard - not simply to give the law priority. If the Code is more demanding than local law on some point, a CFA member still has to follow the Code.
Standard I(C): Misrepresentation - not only about recommendations

Many people assume misrepresentation is only about how an investment is described. In fact the Standard reaches much further: it covers false claims about education, work experience and professional credentials, including your progress through the CFA exams, in your own personal profile. That is why CFA Institute deals so severely with candidates who overstate their exam progress on LinkedIn or a CV.
Standard I(D): Misconduct - reaching beyond the job

Misconduct has the widest reach in the group. It is not confined to conduct at work: it covers personal conduct too, social media included, where that conduct bears on honesty and trustworthiness and could damage the reputation of the investment profession as a whole.

sections.label: An important distinction
sections.text: Standard I(C) is about MISSTATING a specific piece of information (a CV, an investment recommendation), while Standard I(D) is about UNPROFESSIONAL CONDUCT in general (dishonesty, fraud) that need not involve any specific statement at all.
Standard II: from inside information to market manipulation

Standard II(A) - Material Nonpublic Information prohibits trading or making recommendations on material information that has not been made public. Standard II(B) - Market Manipulation is broader than most people assume: beyond spreading false rumours, it covers trading techniques that artificially distort price or volume, such as placing fake orders (spoofing) to fake supply or demand.

items: Standard I(A): always apply whichever is stricter, the law or the Code of Ethics
Standard I(B): avoid both an actual conflict of interest and the outward appearance of one
Standard I(C): covers misstatements about investments and about your own qualifications alike
Standard I(D): the widest reach, including conduct outside work that affects the profession's reputation
Standard II(B): includes artificial trading techniques (spoofing), not just false rumours

lines: Telling the sub-standards apart reliably takes practice across varied situations, not memorising the names.
In the next lesson we carry on with in-depth case studies for Standards III and IV.
